# Disagreement Log — Acts of Thomas, Chapter 2
**Agents:** EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 11

---

## Verse-by-Verse Disagreements

### v.1 — Travel description
- **EMET:** "went together to a certain city of India"
- **LOGOS:** "traveled to a certain city in India"
- **PNEUMA:** "sailed for India" (adds sea voyage)
- **Note:** PNEUMA's "sailed" adds a travel detail not in the source chapter. The text does not describe the journey in this chapter.

### v.5 — "played the flute before them" vs. "playing before the guests"
- **EMET:** "played the flute before them"
- **LOGOS:** "playing before the guests"
- **PNEUMA:** "working the crowd" (idiomatic addition)
- **Note:** "Working the crowd" (PNEUMA) is a modern idiom not in source.

### v.6 — "was of the Hebrew race" vs. "of Hebrew origin" vs. "was Jewish"
- **EMET:** "was of the Hebrew race"
- **LOGOS:** "was of Hebrew origin"
- **PNEUMA:** "was Jewish"
- **Note:** "Jewish" (PNEUMA) is an anachronistic term in this context; "Hebrew" (*'Ibrayya* in Syriac) is the text's own word.

### v.7 — "loved him greatly and was held fast by him"
- **EMET:** "loved him greatly and was held fast by him"
- **LOGOS:** "was deeply drawn to him"
- **PNEUMA:** "was captivated"
- **Note:** EMET preserves both dimensions — active love and passive captivation. LOGOS and PNEUMA collapse to one element each.

### v.8 — "came and smote Thomas on the cheek" vs. "struck Thomas on the cheek" vs. "slapped Thomas across the cheek"
- **EMET:** "came and smote Thomas on the cheek"
- **LOGOS:** "came and struck Thomas on the cheek"
- **PNEUMA:** "slapped Thomas across the cheek"
- **Note:** "Smote" (EMET) is archaic. "Struck" (LOGOS) is neutral. "Slapped" (PNEUMA) diminishes the severity of the blow.

### v.9 — "My God will forgive this smiting" vs. "My God will forgive this blow"
- **EMET:** "forgive this smiting"
- **LOGOS:** "forgive this blow"
- **PNEUMA:** "forgive that blow"
- **Note:** "Smiting" (EMET) is archaic; "blow" (LOGOS) is standard. PNEUMA's "that" shifts to past-tense reference — minor.

### v.9 — "dragged by dogs" vs. "I shall see that hand... dragged by dogs"
- **EMET:** "I shall see that hand which smote me dragged by dogs"
- **LOGOS/PNEUMA:** "that hand which struck me dragged by dogs"
- **Note:** All agree on the image; minor verb disagreements only.

### v.10 — "struck him down and killed him" vs. "came out of nowhere" (PNEUMA addition)
- **EMET/LOGOS:** "a lion struck him down and killed him"
- **PNEUMA:** "A lion came out of nowhere, struck him down, and killed him"
- **Note:** "Out of nowhere" (PNEUMA) adds dramatic surprise not in source.

### v.10 — "the dogs dragged him" vs. "dogs tore at his body"
- **EMET:** "the dogs dragged him"
- **LOGOS:** "dogs tore at his body"
- **PNEUMA:** same as LOGOS
- **Note:** "Dragged" (EMET) is more literal; "tore at" (LOGOS) adds graphic specificity not explicit in source.

### v.11 — "inquired who it was that had prophesied" vs. "asked who it was that had spoken this prophecy"
- **EMET:** "inquired who it was that had prophesied this"
- **LOGOS:** "asked who it was that had spoken this prophecy"
- **PNEUMA:** "who had prophesied this? Who had known?"
- **Note:** PNEUMA adds a second question ("who had known?") not in source.

### v.12 — "broke her flute" — all agents agree. The symbolic gesture (destroying her professional instrument) is preserved by all.

---
*11 disagreements. SOPHIA: "struck" (v.8); retain both "loved" and "held fast" (v.7); "Hebrew origin" (v.6); reject "came out of nowhere" (v.10).*
